scenes.text: The first close up picture of Mars was colored in by hand, with pastels.
On November twenty eighth, nineteen sixty four, NASA launched Mariner four toward Mars.
Its twin, Mariner three, had failed weeks earlier when its nose cover wouldn't come off.
Mariner four flew for two hundred twenty eight days to reach the red planet.
In July nineteen sixty five, it passed about six thousand miles above the surface.
It snapped twenty two photos and stored them on tape.
Its radio sent the data home at just over eight bits per second.
Each photo took around ten hours to arrive.
Engineers at JPL were too impatient to wait for the computer to draw the first one.
So a machine printed the brightness values as numbers on strips of paper.
They lined the strips up side by side and colored them like a paint by numbers.
The finished picture was framed and given to JPL's director.
The photos showed a cold, dry Mars covered in craters, a lot like our Moon.
Its radio signal also revealed that the air pressure on Mars is only about one percent of Earth's.
Would you have waited ten hours, or grabbed the pastels too? Comment below.

title: The first close-up of Mars was colored by hand 🖍️
caption: Mariner 4 launched on Nov 28, 1964 and sent back the first close-up photos of Mars at about 8 bits per second. JPL engineers couldn't wait, so they colored the first image by hand from printed numbers.
